title: Vectors | Chapter 1, Essence of linear algebra
summary: The first chapter of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, introducing vectors with animated geometric visuals. It begins a series that builds intuition for linear algebra from the basics.
why_hn: HN's go-to recommendation for learning linear algebra intuition, repeatedly credited with making concepts click and complementing textbooks.

quote.text: the most welcoming and informative introduction to the topic I've ever seen

title: Ruby Conf 12 - Y Not- Adventures in Functional Programming by Jim Weirich
summary: Jim Weirich's RubyConf 2012 talk derives the Y combinator step by step, live-coding in Ruby lambdas. It builds up an understanding of functional programming and lambda calculus from first principles.
why_hn: HN recommends it repeatedly as one of the best and most entertaining programming talks, and as the talk that makes the Y combinator click, even for people who do not use Ruby.

quote.text: perhaps the most entertaining and interesting technical talk I've ever seen.

title: Indistinguishable From Magic: Manufacturing Modern Computer Chips
summary: A HOPE09 talk on how modern computer chips are manufactured, from 22nm transistors to ultra-clean fabs and the tricks used to pattern tiny features with light. It frames chipmaking as hacking electrical engineering and physics.
why_hn: HN repeatedly calls it the best in-depth introduction to IC manufacturing, a sense-of-awe talk by an independent engineer, while wishing for an updated version.

quote.text: This talk on YouTube is the most in depth explanation of IC manufacuring I have seen. I highly recommend it to anyone, no matter their background.

title: How to Speak
summary: Patrick Winston's long-running MIT lecture on public speaking teaches heuristic rules for talks. It covers how to start, use time and place, boards, props and slides, and how to inform, persuade and finish.
why_hn: HN treats it as the canonical, near-universally recommended lecture on giving talks and presentations.

quote.text: drop what you're doing and watch it now

title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
summary: Andrej Karpathy's first Neural Networks: Zero to Hero lecture, which builds micrograd, a tiny autograd engine, from scratch in Python. It explains backpropagation and neural network training step by step, assuming only basic Python and some high-school calculus.
why_hn: HN treats it as the best starting point for really understanding backprop and neural nets, because Karpathy explains the why with intuition and builds everything in code.

quote.text: It's especially useful because he explains the why and provides intuitive explanations instead of just talking about the what and how.

title: 8 Bit & '8 Bitish' Graphics-Outside the Box
summary: Mark Ferrari, the LucasArts background artist, explains in a GDC 2016 talk how he draws 8-bit graphics. He covers color cycling and palette shifting to create complex animated scenery without frame animation.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as a master class in limited-palette pixel art and palette cycling, from an artist behind Loom and Monkey Island.

quote.text: I recommend this talk to anyone who is interested in the details and history of working on limited colour palette games!

title: How Python was Shaped by leaky Internals, Armin Ronacher, Flask framework
summary: Armin Ronacher, creator of Flask, explains how CPython's internals and C API leak into the language's semantics. Using examples like the complexity of the add operation, he shows why Python is hard to optimize or reimplement.
why_hn: It is HN's standard answer to why Python cannot easily get much faster, and is recommended by people who work on JITs and alternative runtimes.

quote.text: This excellent talk describes how the semantics of the "add" operation are much more complex than generally described.

title: AT&T Archives: Similiarities of Wave Behavior (Bonus Edition)
summary: A Bell Labs film in which Dr. J.N. Shive uses a mechanical wave machine to demonstrate reflection, standing waves, resonance and impedance matching. He includes some equations but relies mostly on real-world examples a layperson can follow.
why_hn: HN repeatedly calls it the clearest introduction to waves and transmission-line behavior, better than modern explainers.

quote.text: By far the best introduction to the subject of waves of any sort.

title: In Search Of A Flat Earth
summary: Dan Olson's 76-minute essay on flat earth belief, built around a hike to a lake to test earth's curvature. It examines the community, how YouTube promoted it, and how it connects to wider conspiracy thinking and QAnon.
why_hn: HN treats it as the definitive, compassionate documentary on why people fall into conspiracy theories.

quote.text: probably the best documentary I have seen on conspiracy theories.

title: 1. Introduction to Human Behavioral Biology
summary: The opening lecture of Robert Sapolsky's Stanford course on Human Behavioral Biology, explaining the course premise and how to avoid categorical thinking. It starts a roughly 25-lecture series on how biology, genes, hormones and environment shape behavior.
why_hn: One of the most consistently recommended lecture series on HN, praised as fascinating, funny and eye-opening about human behavior across many scales.

quote.text: Best course I've ever done.

title: How The Economic Machine Works by Ray Dalio
summary: Ray Dalio's 30-minute animated video explains how the economy works through credit, debt, interest rates, and short- and long-term cycles. It is based on his template for understanding the economy.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the best layperson overview of debt, credit and economic cycles.

quote.text: it’s the best layperson explanation of debt I’ve ever seen

title: RailsConf 2014 - All the Little Things by Sandi Metz
summary: Sandi Metz takes an ugly section of conditional code and refactors it into a few simple objects, bridging object-oriented theory and practice. The talk includes her take on the Gilded Rose refactoring kata and the idea that duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.
why_hn: HN treats it as a top-tier programming talk for learning refactoring and for the wrong-abstraction principle, recommended repeatedly over a decade.

quote.text: this talk captures all the important values in a single example.

title: But what is the Fourier Transform?  A visual introduction.
summary: 3Blue1Brown's animated visual introduction to the Fourier Transform, showing how a signal breaks into frequency components.
why_hn: HN's default recommendation for understanding the Fourier transform intuitively; many say it was the explanation that made it click.

quote.text: this was the first thing that ever really made sense to me

title: Around The Corner - How Differential Steering Works (1937)
summary: A 1937 GM-produced film explaining how the automobile differential lets wheels turn at different speeds around a corner. It uses clear animations and cutaway demonstrations to build the idea from first principles.
why_hn: Held up as a marvel of pedagogy and the best explanation of differentials, recommended again and again.

quote.text: this video explaining differentials is from 1937 and is a marvel of pedagogy

title: The Soul of Erlang and Elixir • Sasa Juric • GOTO 2019
summary: Sasa Juric explains what makes Erlang and Elixir suited to server-side systems, focusing on the BEAM concurrency model rather than syntax or ecosystem. He demonstrates processes, supervision, and fault tolerance.
why_hn: It is HN's favorite pitch for Elixir and the BEAM, credited with convincing many people to adopt them.

quote.text: Watch this if you want to understand why so many people fall in love with it.

title: Essential Ideas for Parents
summary: Dr. Russell Barkley's roughly three-hour lecture on ADHD for parents of affected children. It explains what ADHD is and how the ADHD brain differs.
why_hn: Repeatedly called the best way to understand ADHD, and recommended to anyone before commenting on it.

quote.text: Here's the best explanation I've ever seen of the subject

title: "Simple Made Easy" - Rich Hickey (2011)
summary: Rich Hickey's Strange Loop 2011 keynote distinguishing 'simple' (not intertwined) from 'easy' (familiar or near at hand). It argues that software complexity comes from complecting things and that we should pick simple constructs.
why_hn: HN treats it as the canonical talk on software complexity, shared constantly and recommended to every programmer regardless of language.

quote.text: is a must-watch (even if you never touch Clojure)

title: The Quantum Conspiracy: What Popularizers of QM Don't Want You to Know
summary: Ron Garret's Google Tech Talk argues that quantum mechanics is no harder to understand than relativity and that popular accounts wrongly rely on the Copenhagen interpretation. He presents measurement as entanglement and explains phenomena like the quantum eraser.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the talk that finally made quantum mechanics click, especially for programmers.

quote.text: This is the video that finally made it click for me[1].

title: Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown
summary: CGP Grey's animated adaptation of The Dictator's Handbook, explaining how rulers stay in power by keeping a small group of key supporters happy rather than ruling fairly. It lays out selectorate theory and how resources shape regimes.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard short summary of how power and political incentives work, applied to governments, companies and workplaces.

quote.text: CGP Grey's excellent Rules for Rulers video

title: LEADERSHIP LAB: The Craft of Writing Effectively
summary: Larry McEnerney of the University of Chicago Writing Program gives a graduate-student session on writing effectively. His core idea is that readers care about value to them, not the writer's thinking process.
why_hn: HN users repeatedly say it changed how they think about writing, calling it a masterclass useful far beyond academia.

quote.text: it's a masterclass in understanding what writing actually is, and what it does for you

title: What the heck is the event loop anyway? | Philip Roberts | JSConf EU
summary: Philip Roberts explains the JavaScript event loop, call stack, callbacks and asynchronous behavior with live visualizations using a tool he built. It demystifies terms like non-blocking and single-threaded.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly name it as the best explanation of the JS event loop and the first thing to watch before tackling async code.

quote.text: The tool he created to display the event loop in real time is fantastic.

title: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
summary: 3Blue1Brown's first chapter on deep learning explains what neurons and layers are and the math underlying a basic neural network, using handwritten digit recognition with visual animations.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard first stop for learning neural networks, praised for making the math intuitive.

quote.text: the visualisations and explanations of the math/concepts are so amazing

title: A Better Default Colormap for Matplotlib | SciPy 2015 | Nathaniel Smith and Stéfan van der Walt
summary: SciPy 2015 talk by Nathaniel Smith and Stefan van der Walt on choosing a new default colormap for Matplotlib. It covers why Jet misleads, how perceptual color spaces work, and how viridis was designed.
why_hn: HN's go-to recommendation for colormap and color-perception questions; commenters call it funny, brief, clear and a favorite talk.

quote.text: This hilarious SciPy2015 talk[1] convinced me to switch to the Parula color scheme.

title: George Lakoff: Moral Politics
summary: Cognitive scientist George Lakoff lectures on how political debates are framed through language and metaphors tied to values, and on the moral worldviews behind progressive and conservative politics. It was given in 2005 at UC San Diego.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly say it changed how they hear political speech and recommend it for understanding why opponents are not simply stupid.

quote.text: Changed how I listen - to anyone - forever.

title: Heat Pumps: the Future of Home Heating
summary: Technology Connections explains how heat pumps work as reversed air conditioners and why they can deliver several times the heat of resistive heating per unit of energy. It also tackles common myths such as poor cold-weather performance.
why_hn: HN's default recommendation for a friendly, thorough introduction to heat pumps and why they are so efficient.

quote.text: Start here for a good introduction to heat pumps and how they are so efficient

title: Micro Men - 720p (2009)
summary: Micro Men is a 2009 BBC comic drama about the early 1980s British home computer boom. It follows the rivalry between Clive Sinclair and Acorn founder Chris Curry over the BBC Micro contract and the ZX Spectrum.
why_hn: HN recommends it often as an entertaining and authentic dramatization of Sinclair versus Acorn, the story from which ARM grew.

quote.text: 'Micro Men' is an excellent TV drama

title: The Beauty of Bézier Curves
summary: Freya Holmer explains how Bezier curves work, from the helper-line construction to their uses in animation, text rendering and shapes. It uses visuals from her Unity Shapes plugin and was a SoME1 contest winner.
why_hn: HN repeatedly calls it one of the best math and graphics explainers on YouTube, praised for bridging game dev and math.

quote.text: it's genuinely one of the best math/graphics/explainer videos ever made

title: The Century of the Self (Full Adam Curtis Documentary)
summary: Adam Curtis' multi-part documentary on how Freud's ideas and Edward Bernays' public relations shaped consumer culture and political control. It argues that business and government learned to manufacture desires.
why_hn: HN recommends it often and strongly as an eye-opening account of marketing psychology and the engineering of consumer society.

quote.text: For the first time in my life I feel like I understood the “why” of how things work in American society.

title: The Tragedy of systemd
summary: FreeBSD developer Benno Rice traces the history of init and bootstrap systems at linux.conf.au 2019 to explain why systemd was seen as necessary and why it provokes such strong reactions. He also discusses why change is scary.
why_hn: The most-recommended balanced take on systemd, from a BSD perspective, handed to anyone caught up in the systemd debate.

quote.text: is an interesting talk on this topic from the view of someone (Benno Rice) in BSD land. Highly recommended.

title: Rich Harris - Rethinking reactivity
summary: Svelte creator Rich Harris explains moving reactivity into the compiler and language rather than tracking state at runtime, with a history of spreadsheets as reactive systems and comparisons to React.
why_hn: The most recommended introduction to Svelte, credited with sparking its adoption.

quote.text: you can (and I heartily recommend doing so) watch the "Rethinking reactivity" video here

title: "Making Impossible States Impossible" by Richard Feldman
summary: Richard Feldman's elm-conf talk on designing models so that bugs from impossible application states cannot occur, using Elm's compiler and types. It demonstrates techniques for making invalid states unrepresentable.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as a talk that changed how people model data, with ideas that apply well beyond Elm to any typed language.

quote.text: the talk is Elm lang focused, but the concepts still apply to other languages.

title: Dominion (2018) - full documentary [Official]
summary: Dominion is a two-hour documentary using drones and hidden cameras to expose conditions in animal agriculture, including food, clothing, entertainment and research. It questions humanity's dominion over animals.
why_hn: HN commenters push it, often forcefully, as the video to watch to see what factory farming really involves, and some say it changed their diet.

quote.text: this documentary made me re-evaluate my diet.

title: D/A and A/D | Digital Show and Tell (Monty Montgomery @ xiph.org)
summary: Monty Montgomery of Xiph.org gives real-time demonstrations of sampling, quantization, bit depth and dither using real audio equipment, including both digital analysis tools and vintage analog bench gear. It shows that sampled audio is not stair-stepped and corrects common misconceptions about digital audio.
why_hn: HN calls it the gold-standard debunking of audiophile myths and the stair-step misconception, and recommends it as a primer on digital audio.

quote.text: might be the best explanatory video I have ever witnessed

title: SM64 - Watch for Rolling Rocks - 0.5x A Presses (Commentated) [OUTDATED]
summary: Pannenkoek2012's commentated tool-assisted Super Mario 64 run collecting the Watch for Rolling Rocks star with half an A press, using parallel universes and QPU movement. The video is marked outdated in favor of a newer version.
why_hn: Held up as a legendary deep dive into game internals, explained lucidly and with humor, and a gateway to the channel.

quote.text: This guy literally has a PhD in SM64. It's insanely complicated, and surprisingly lucid.

title: 8-bit computer update
summary: Ben Eater's short update announcing his plan to build another 8-bit computer from scratch on camera. It kicks off the breadboard computer series that became widely known.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends the series it launched as the best way to understand how a CPU works, praised for Eater's clear teaching.

quote.text: I think I learned more from Ben Eater’s “Building an 8-bit breadboard computer” series [0] than my intro to computer architecture course at university.

title: MIT's Pathway to Fusion Energy (IAP 2017) - Zach Hartwig
channel: MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center
summary: Zach Hartwig of MIT introduces the key concepts of magnetic fusion energy and the state of fusion research. He then presents MIT's proposed pathway of using high-field superconducting magnets to build smaller, cheaper tokamaks on a climate-relevant timescale.
why_hn: Recommended again and again as the best accessible overview of fusion physics, useful for judging fusion announcements and understanding why high-temperature superconducting magnets matter.

quote.text: This has been by far the most informative source on Fusion I've seen and gives a clear picture on how to evaluate claims like this.

title: Stanford's Sapolsky On Depression in U.S. (Full Lecture)
summary: Stanford professor Robert Sapolsky lectures on depression as a real biological disease. He covers its biological and psychological causes, how it differs from ordinary sadness, and ideas such as learned helplessness. He ties these together into one account.
why_hn: HN returns to it repeatedly as the best single introduction to understanding clinical depression.

quote.text: This is the quintessential video for understanding clinical depression.

title: The Continuity of Splines
summary: Freya Holmer's 74-minute video essay on splines, covering Bezier curves, B-splines, derivatives and the different levels of continuity (C0, C1, C2), built with custom animation tools. She notes she did not cover non-uniform splines.
why_hn: It is the go-to recommendation for anyone who wants to genuinely understand Bezier curves and splines, and commenters repeatedly call it one of the best programming-related educational videos.

quote.text: is (IMHO) one of the best educational videos on a programming topic, full stop.

title: Justice: What's The Right Thing To Do? Episode 01 "THE MORAL SIDE OF MURDER"
summary: The first episode of Michael Sandel's Harvard course on moral reasoning, opening with the trolley problem and the choice between killing one to save five. Sandel draws out student arguments and introduces utilitarian and other approaches to justice.
why_hn: One of the most frequently recommended online lecture series on HN, praised for giving people vocabulary to examine ethical positions and for Sandel's skilled teaching.

quote.text: Two lecture series I always recommend, and feel like everyone should watch

title: Video explains the world's most important 6-sec drum loop
summary: Nate Harrison's 2004 video history of the Amen Break, a six-second drum sample from a 1969 b-side that became the basis of hip-hop sampling, jungle and drum and bass. It is also a meditation on cultural ownership and creativity.
why_hn: A perennial HN recommendation, brought up whenever sampling, copyright or music history comes up, often described as a must-watch.

quote.text: this is an excellent 20-minute video about the history of the Amen Break

title: CppCon 2015: Andrei Alexandrescu “std::allocator...”
summary: Andrei Alexandrescu's CppCon 2015 talk argues that std::allocator is badly designed. He proposes building high-performance allocators from small composable, templated pieces.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as an entertaining, mind-opening talk on allocator design and composable generic programming.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: It really opened my eyes to how one could very elegantly make a very complex and high-performance heap allocator

title: Jim Simons (full length interview) - Numberphile
summary: The full-length Numberphile interview with mathematician and hedge fund founder Jim Simons. He discusses his path from mathematics and codebreaking to founding Renaissance Technologies, his use of algorithms in markets, and his philanthropy.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the best readily available interview with Simons, notable for his emphasis on luck and a humble approach to success.

quote.text: the full length one is very good. it gives an understanding as to why simons has been so successful.

title: Reverse emulating the NES to give it SUPER POWERS!
summary: Tom Murphy (suckerpinch) shows 'reverse emulation', using a Raspberry Pi in an NES cartridge to give an unmodified NES new abilities such as playing SNES games. The video starts in a strange way and gets stranger.
why_hn: Praised as a brilliant, deadpan and inventive hardware hack, and a good starting point for Tom7's videos.

quote.text: are a must watch.

title: Sugar: THE BITTER TRUTH
summary: Robert Lustig of UCSF lectures on the biochemistry of sugar, arguing that fructose and lack of fiber drive the obesity epidemic via insulin. It is the widely viewed 90-minute talk that popularized the anti-sugar case.
why_hn: The most-linked YouTube video on HN, recommended as an in-depth explanation of fructose metabolism.

quote.text: This is one of the best nutritional videos I've ever seen.

title: Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business with Jason Cohen
summary: Jason Cohen's MicroConf talk on designing a bootstrapped business by starting from your own strengths, goals and constraints. He works backward to the business model, pricing, market and product that fit, with practical points like annual prepay and pricing tiers.
why_hn: It is the go-to talk HN commenters recommend to anyone asking about bootstrapping, SaaS pricing, or choosing bootstrapping over VC.

quote.text: This talk is the holy grail on this topic

title: How Self-Driving Cars will Destroy Cities (and what to do about it)
summary: Not Just Bikes argues that self-driving cars will worsen sprawl and car dependence and harm cities. The video compares car-centered and people-centered urban design and weighs what cities should do instead.
why_hn: Frequently recommended in autonomous vehicle and Waymo threads as the main counterargument, a long but worthwhile video essay on how self-driving cars could affect cities.

quote.text: It's long, but well worth an hour of your time.

title: Light Years Ahead | The 1969 Apollo Guidance Computer
summary: Robert Wills of TNMoC explains the Apollo Guidance Computer hardware and software, then walks through the Apollo 11 landing procedure step by step, including the 1202 alarms.
why_hn: HN calls it mandatory viewing on the AGC, praising the speaker's enthusiasm and the clear account of restartable, robust software design.

quote.text: The guy is really, really into it and it just makes the presentation amazing.

title: Steve Jobs Stanford Commencement Speech 2005
summary: Steve Jobs's 2005 Stanford commencement address, built around three stories: connecting the dots, love and loss including being fired from Apple, and death. It is a 15-minute talk on finding work you love.
why_hn: HN returns to it for years as an inspirational talk to send to graduates, founders and anyone at a career crossroads.

quote.text: This is no doubt one of the best speech i ever heard.

title: Quantum Computing for Computer Scientists
summary: An 88-minute Microsoft Research talk that explains how quantum computers beat classical ones using basic linear algebra, qubits, superposition and gates. It works through the Deutsch oracle problem and ends with entanglement, teleportation and a live demo.
why_hn: It is HN's most frequently recommended starting point for quantum computing because it avoids pop-science hand-waving and needs only basic linear algebra.

quote.text: This video is the simplest explanation that I have found for Quantum Computing

title: Juice it or lose it - a talk by Martin Jonasson & Petri Purho
summary: Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho take a bland Breakout clone and add layer after layer of 'juice' such as easing, particles, screen shake and sound until it feels alive. A live demo makes the effect of small feedback details obvious.
why_hn: The go-to recommendation on game feel and polish, cited by HN as one of the best talks for anyone making interactive things feel good.

quote.text: Gotta be one of the best talks for anyone trying to make things interactive that also feel good.

title: Lexical Scanning in Go - Rob Pike
summary: Rob Pike shows how the Go text/template lexer is built, using state functions, goroutines and channels. The talk was given at a Google Technology User Group in Sydney in 2011.
why_hn: HN returns to it for years as an elegant introduction to writing a lexer that is easy to follow even without a parsing background.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: It's far more interesting than it sounds, and even if you don't know much about lexing/parsing it's easy to follow.

title: “Hello, world” from scratch on a 6502 — Part 1
summary: Ben Eater starts a series building a working computer on breadboards around the 6502 microprocessor. In this first part he gets a 'hello world' running from scratch.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the best hands-on way to understand how a CPU and a computer work from first principles.

quote.text: It is highly recommended if you want to dive down into computers and digital logic on first principles.

title: William Byrd on "The Most Beautiful Program Ever Written" [PWL NYC]
summary: William Byrd presents at Papers We Love NYC on what he calls the most beautiful program ever written, a Lisp interpreter written in Lisp. He walks through the metacircular interpreter and related ideas, and demos relational programming and program synthesis near the end.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as an amazing talk that derives the essence of Lisp and shows miniKanren-style program synthesis.

quote.text: I can't recommend the talk Dr Byrd did on this enough

title: What Bodies Think About: Bioelectric Computation Outside the Nervous System - NeurIPS 2018
summary: Michael Levin's NeurIPS 2018 talk on bioelectric computation outside the nervous system, showing how cell electrical networks shape development and regeneration. It covers morphological information processing in living tissue.
why_hn: HN regularly calls it mind-blowing and recommends it as an introduction to Levin's work on bioelectricity and regeneration.

quote.text: I highly recommend this video from Levin. It was my introduction to his work.

title: Lec 1 | MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra, Spring 2005
summary: The first lecture of Gilbert Strang's MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra course, covering the geometry of linear equations. It opens a full 35-lecture university course.
why_hn: It is HN's default recommendation for learning linear algebra, praised for Strang's teaching and for building real understanding useful in machine learning.

quote.text: I highly recommend the MIT 18.06 open course on linear algebra - the lectures are first rate.

title: Detergent packs are kinda wishy-washy (Dishwashers Explained)
summary: Technology Connections explains how dishwashers work, why detergent pods underperform powder, and how to use the pre-wash and main-wash compartments. It argues you don't need to pre-rinse dishes.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the definitive, mind-changing explanation of dishwasher use, even though it runs over 30 minutes.

quote.text: I highly recommend you watch this video by Technology connections[1], I too used to think I had to rinse my dishes before putting them in the machine.

title: "Testing Distributed Systems w/ Deterministic Simulation" by Will Wilson
summary: Will Wilson of FoundationDB explains how the team tested their distributed database using deterministic simulation. By running the whole system in a simulator with injected faults and reproducible seeds, they could find rare concurrency and network bugs.
why_hn: HN treats it as the canonical talk on simulation testing and a mind-blowing example of how far rigorous testing can go.

quote.text: this is one of the most amazing talks on distributed systems

title: What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us
summary: CGP Grey's video "Humans Need Not Apply" argues that automation will make a large part of the workforce economically obsolete, much as engines did for horses. It surveys robots and software replacing both physical and mental labor.
why_hn: HN has recommended it for a decade as the standard explainer on automation and unemployment, though skeptics later cite it as an example of overconfident predictions.

quote.text: Excellent video on the subject: CGPGrey - Humans Need Not Apply

title: Behind the Scenes of iOS Security
summary: Apple security head Ivan Krstic gives a Black Hat 2016 talk on iOS security, covering HomeKit, Auto Unlock and iCloud Keychain. He explains key hierarchies and how data can stay safe even in adversarial clouds.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the deepest public look at how iCloud Keychain and Apple's device and cloud security are designed.

quote.text: if you haven't watched the talk at Black Hat I'd highly recommend it

title: 🚀  TDD, Where Did It All Go Wrong (Ian Cooper)
summary: Ian Cooper's DevTernity talk revisits Kent Beck's original TDD ideas and shows where misunderstandings crept in. It argues tests should target behaviors through public interfaces rather than implementation details, so suites support refactoring instead of resisting it.
why_hn: HN repeatedly calls it the best talk on testing, and many say it changed how they approach tests, mocks and the meaning of a unit.

quote.text: This excellent talk completely changed the way I approached testing. Every developer who writes tests needs to watch this now!

title: Bret Victor - Inventing on Principle
summary: Bret Victor's talk at CUSEC 2012 in which he argues that creators need immediate feedback and should organize their work around a guiding principle. He demonstrates live-coding and animation tools that show results as you type, and describes his own principle that creators must see what they are making.
why_hn: It is HN's go-to recommendation for the case that programming environments should give instant feedback, and it appears in nearly every thread on live coding, visual programming or developer tools.

quote.text: My mind was blown when I saw this video 2 years ago

title: This Is Phil Fish
summary: Innuendo Studios uses Phil Fish, creator of the game Fez, as a case study in internet celebrity. The essay argues that fame online works differently from traditional fame, and shows how audiences turn on the people they have elevated.
why_hn: Commenters repeatedly name it the best explanation of how internet fame, mobs and outrage work, and cite it in threads about harassment and public figures.

quote.text: possibly the most important video on youtube - is "This Is Phil Fish"[1] by Innuendo Studios.

title: James Burke Connections, Ep. 1 "The Trigger Effect"
summary: The first episode of James Burke's 1978 BBC series Connections traces modern dependence on complex technological networks, starting with the 1965 New York blackout, and moves through ancient agriculture to Kuwait's oil-driven leap.
why_hn: Heavily recommended as a masterpiece of popular science and the classic illustration of how fragile interdependent systems are, trotted out in every blackout or supply chain thread.

quote.text: It's a masterpiece of popular science production made better with the grainy film patina of the 70s and 80s.

title: How To Design A Good API and Why it Matters
summary: Joshua Bloch's Google Tech Talk on how to design good APIs and why it matters, with concrete principles and examples. It treats every programmer as an occasional API designer.
why_hn: HN repeatedly names it the best resource on API design, a staple answer to any 'how do I design an API' question.

quote.text: Absolutely far and away the best resource that I found was this Google TechTalk by Joshua Bloch

title: elevated by Rgba & TBC | 4k intro (FullHD 1080p demoscene demo)
summary: Elevated by Rgba and TBC, the winner of the 4k intro compo at Breakpoint 2009. It is a realtime procedurally generated 3D flythrough with music, all in a 4096-byte executable.
why_hn: Held up as the landmark demoscene production and a counterpoint to software bloat.

quote.text: It demonstrated that 4k was more than sufficient for impressive effects and music

title: Hans Rosling's 200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes - The Joy of Stats - BBC
summary: Hans Rosling uses augmented-reality animation to show 200 countries over 200 years in four minutes, built from 120,000 data points. It tracks life expectancy and income to show the world's development.
why_hn: HN commenters send it as a short antidote to cynicism, showing long-term global progress and the shrinking gap between rich and poor countries.

quote.text: Spend five minutes and watch this. Amazing presentation my Hans Rausling

title: Mechanical Computer (All Parts) - Basic Mechanisms In Fire Control Computers
summary: A 1953 US Navy training film explaining the basic mechanisms in mechanical fire control computers aboard ships. It shows how gears, differentials and cams solved mathematical problems in permanent mechanical form.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as a beautiful, approachable explanation of analog mechanical computation, and many have rewatched it.

quote.text: It illustrates the problems and solutions near perfectly, and I've watched it way too many times.

title: The Problem with Time & Timezones - Computerphile
summary: Tom Scott explains for Computerphile why handling time and timezones in code is so hard, walking through a simple web app that computes how long ago something happened. It covers the quirks of timezones and calendars and ends in an exasperated rant.
why_hn: It is the go-to funny, accessible explanation of why you should never implement datetime handling yourself, linked in nearly every timezone thread.

quote.text: a must watch for developers just starting out with Timezones

title: The Value of Values with Rich Hickey
summary: Rich Hickey's JaxConf 2012 keynote examines what values are and why immutable values matter as information systems grow more complex and data gets bigger. It contrasts places with values and builds the case for immutability.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as the talk that convinced them of immutability and functional programming.

quote.text: is what finally sold me on the benefits of pure functional programming and immutable data structures.

title: Project Code Rush - The Beginnings of Netscape / Mozilla Documentary
summary: Code Rush is a one-hour documentary following Netscape engineers in Silicon Valley through the company's last year as an independent firm. It covers the Mozilla open-source announcement, the frantic push to ready the source for release by March 31, 1998, and the toll on engineers' lives before the AOL acquisition.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an intimate, embedded look at late-90s web history and the spirit of building something important under pressure.

quote.text: Code Rush, which is an awesome documentary for anyone interested in the history of the Web

title: Bret Victor   The Future of Programming
summary: Bret Victor's DBX 2013 talk, delivered in the guise of a 1973 IBM engineer with an overhead projector. It surveys forgotten ideas from 1960s and early 70s computing and warns against assuming you know what you're doing.
why_hn: HN treats it as a classic, near-mandatory talk on how programming tools and paradigms stagnated and which older ideas deserve revival.

quote.text: Take a look and you will be amazed of how good (or revolutionary by our standards) some old technologies were.

title: Jan Willem Nijman - Vlambeer - "The art of screenshake" at INDIGO Classes 2013
summary: Vlambeer's Jan Willem Nijman shows how to make an action game feel great by stacking small effects like screenshake, recoil and particles onto a basic shooter. It was presented at INDIGO Classes 2013.
why_hn: A perennial recommendation for anyone learning game feel and juice, praised for showing concrete steps that turn a bland prototype into a satisfying game.

title: DON'T PANIC — Hans Rosling showing the facts about population
summary: Hans Rosling uses data and animated statistics to show how world population is changing, why birth rates fall as child survival and wealth rise, and why population is expected to peak around 11 billion. It also tackles common misconceptions about Africa and family planning.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it to counter overpopulation alarm with data on falling birth rates.

quote.text: I can highly recommend this lecture by the late Hans Rosling

title: Music Theory and White Supremacy
summary: Adam Neely examines Phil Ewell's paper arguing Western music theory is framed by a white racial perspective. He covers North Indian theory, alternative frameworks, Schenker and responses to the paper.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the canonical video on how music theory is really the theory of one Western tradition, with the raga example.

quote.text: The canonical video on the subject

title: Why Electronic Voting Is Still A Bad Idea
summary: Tom Scott explains why electronic voting is a bad idea. Elections must be trusted by everyone and attacks on software scale in ways attacks on paper do not, so open source or blockchain fixes do not solve it.
why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to layperson-friendly argument against e-voting and links it in nearly every voting-technology thread.

quote.text: Tom Scott still has the best argument against e-voting IMO [1].

title: Velocity NY 2013:   Richard Cook, "Resilience In Complex Adaptive Systems"
summary: Richard Cook's short Velocity 2013 talk on resilience in complex adaptive systems, arguing systems operate near the edge of failure and that the surprise is how rarely they fail. He presents a model of how pressures push systems toward failure boundaries.
why_hn: HN people cite it constantly as the clearest explanation of normalization of deviance and how complex systems drift toward failure.

quote.text: One of the most important talks I've ever seen is Richard Cook's

title: Why Isn't Functional Programming the Norm? – Richard Feldman
summary: Richard Feldman argues that functional programming is not the norm largely because of historical accidents, such as C++ popularity, platform exclusivity, marketing spend and network effects, rather than merit. He traces the history of how languages become mainstream.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard answer to why FP isn't mainstream and why languages succeed.

quote.text: This talk by Richard Feldman is an excellent discussion about why Functional Programming is not the norm

title: Overwatch Gameplay Architecture and Netcode
summary: Blizzard's Timothy Ford explains in this 2017 GDC session how Overwatch uses an Entity Component System architecture for layered gameplay. He also covers its server-authoritative netcode with client-side prediction and how they keep the game responsive and fair.
why_hn: HN treats it as the best real-world AAA example of ECS and game netcode, and cites it constantly in discussions of data-oriented design.

quote.text: This Overwatch GDC talk is the best breakdown/example of data-oriented ECS in a AAA game that I know of

title: AlphaGo - The Movie | Full award-winning documentary
summary: Feature-length documentary following DeepMind's AlphaGo program as it prepares for and plays the 2016 match against Go champion Lee Sedol. It covers the team, the games, and the emotional reaction of the Go world to an AI beating a top human.
why_hn: HN commenters call it a moving, well-made human story about AI and Go that works for non-technical viewers and does not date.

quote.text: I consider AlphaGo - The Movie [1] to be a timeless classic that will never feel outdated.

title: Maybe Not - Rich Hickey
summary: Rich Hickey's Clojure/Conj 2018 keynote argues that Maybe/Option types and rigid type signatures are a poor way to model data that changes over time. He builds the case around optionality, schema growth and compatibility, and presents the ideas behind Clojure spec as an alternative.
why_hn: HN commenters send people to it whenever nulls, Maybe/Option or static typing come up, as a thoughtful dissent from the type-system orthodoxy that changes how some people model data.

quote.text: Rich Hickey's "Maybe Not" should be watched by anyone who thinks nulls/nils/undefineds are okay.

title: But how does bitcoin actually work?
summary: 3Blue1Brown explains the math and mechanics behind Bitcoin visually: ledgers, digital signatures, proof of work and the blockchain, building up a decentralized payment system from first principles.
why_hn: The go-to recommended video for newcomers wanting a clear, visual explanation of how Bitcoin and blockchains work.

quote.text: this video is the best explanation for how mining and blockchains work IMO

title: We Were Taught to Call Death a Blessing
summary: CGP Grey narrates an animated adaptation of Nick Bostrom's Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant. The story uses a dragon that demands a daily toll of lives as a metaphor for aging and society's acceptance of death.
why_hn: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it in longevity and aging threads as a concise, fun case for fighting aging.

quote.text: CGP gray's videos on YouTube are maybe the most concise and fun to watch materials I've seen on the subject.

title: Don't Talk to the Police
summary: Regent Law professor James Duane gives startling reasons why people, even innocent ones, should always exercise their Fifth Amendment rights rather than talk to police. It is based on his article and book on the subject.
why_hn: HN treats it as the canonical video to link whenever talking to police or interrogations come up.

quote.text: If you don't know why, you must watch this

title: Randy Pausch's Last Lecture: Achieving Your Childhood Dreams
summary: Randy Pausch's 2007 last lecture at Carnegie Mellon, given as he was dying of pancreatic cancer. He reflects on achieving childhood dreams, overcoming obstacles and helping others reach theirs.
why_hn: Perennially recommended as an inspirational talk for people facing setbacks or choosing a direction, and a source of oft-quoted lines like the brick wall.

quote.text: If you haven't watched this, it will change your life.

title: TIMELAPSE OF THE FUTURE: A Journey to the End of Time (4K)
summary: A 29-minute cinematic timelapse by melodysheep that journeys trillions of years into the future, covering the death of the sun, the end of stars, proton decay, black hole evaporation and the fate of the cosmos.
why_hn: HN people recommend it as a stunning, mind-bending and existentially humbling view of deep time, and it appears on lists of favorite YouTube videos.

quote.text: does a great job with visuals and voiceovers about what will happen over the next trillions x trillions of years

title: Treating the Farm as an Ecosystem with Gabe Brown Part 1, The 5 Tenets of Soil Health
summary: A long talk by rancher Gabe Brown on turning his North Dakota farm into a regenerative ecosystem using no-till, cover crops and integrated livestock. It covers the five principles of soil health and how they pay off financially.
why_hn: HN commenters call it their favorite introduction to regenerative agriculture, and several say it changed how they garden or farm.

quote.text: Gabe Brown's talk is my favorite introduction to regenerative ag

title: Solving Problems the Clojure Way - Rafal Dittwald
summary: Rafal Dittwald's Clojure/north talk shows how to move from writing Java-style code in Clojure to thinking in data-driven, functional terms. He walks through a JavaScript example, refactoring imperative code step by step into a functional core.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as a fantastic demonstration of procedural, OOP and FP approaches to the same problem, and of functional core and imperative shell.

quote.text: I urge you to watch this fantastic video which illustrates procedural, OOP(lite), and FP approaches to a sample problem

title: The great porn experiment | Gary Wilson | TEDxGlasgow
summary: Gary Wilson's TEDxGlasgow talk argues that internet pornography hyperstimulates the brain's reward system and can cause symptoms that reverse when people stop. TED notes that several claims are not supported by respected academic studies.
why_hn: HN commenters frequently recommend it as an eye-opening case against heavy porn use, though it is contested science.

quote.text: Here's an enlightening video on the detrimental effects of porn on the brain.

title: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs | Deep Learning Chapter 5
summary: 3Blue1Brown's visual explanation of how transformers and GPT-style language models work, tracing data through tokens, embeddings and attention.
why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to visual introduction to transformers, and many say it finally made attention and embeddings click.

quote.text: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

title: Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order by Ray Dalio
summary: An animated 44-minute summary of Ray Dalio's book Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order. It lays out the Big Cycle of rising and declining nations, covering debt cycles, internal conflict, and shifts in global power over the past 500 years.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a clear framework for placing the current US and world situation within historical debt and empire cycles.

quote.text: definitely watch this video and read Dalio's book (I bought 2 copies)

title: Lecture 1A: Overview and Introduction to Lisp
summary: The first lecture of MIT's 6.001 (SICP) with Abelson and Sussman, giving an overview of the course and an introduction to Lisp. It argues that computer science is about managing complexity and abstraction, not computers.
why_hn: HN people recommend the SICP lectures as a deeper, livelier route into the book and a formative course even for seasoned programmers.

quote.text: I watched and cannot recommend it enough, even for seasoned programmers

title: YouTube's copyright system isn't broken. The world's is.
summary: Tom Scott's long explainer on YouTube's copyright system, Content ID and the DMCA. He argues the platform's system is a workaround for a broader copyright system that does not fit the modern world.
why_hn: The default link in copyright and takedown threads, recommended as an excellent, comprehensive explanation of why automated enforcement and the law work as they do.

quote.text: Tom Scott explains the situation and the solution best.

title: Debugging Under Fire: Keep your Head when Systems have Lost their Mind • Bryan Cantrill • GOTO 2017
summary: Bryan Cantrill's GOTO Chicago 2017 talk on debugging production systems under pressure, centered on the incident where an operator's mistyped command rebooted an entire Joyent datacenter. It covers human factors, automation and architecture.
why_hn: A perennial HN recommendation for outage and postmortem threads, praised as funny, educational and one of the best postmortems anyone has seen.

quote.text: The best postmortem I've seen was actually a conference talk

title: Children Of The Magenta Line
summary: A re-upload of American Airlines captain Warren Vanderburgh's 1997 presentation warning that pilots who over-rely on cockpit automation lose manual flying skills and awareness. The uploader adds context from his own flying.
why_hn: HN brings it up in any thread about autopilot, Tesla FSD, self-driving cars and crashes as the classic lecture on automation dependency.

quote.text: if you haven't seen this amazing talk, you should definitely give it a watch

title: Republic, Lost | Lawrence Lessig | Talks at Google
summary: Lawrence Lessig's Talks at Google presentation based on his book Republic, Lost, arguing that money in politics corrupts Congress and eroded public trust, and outlining what could be done about it. It supports the argument with data on political donations.
why_hn: A perennial HN recommendation whenever lobbying, SOPA, taxes or political corruption come up, with several commenters saying it changed their views.

quote.text: That video has changed my point of view on the entire subject and has allowed me to start striking at the root.

title: London Swallowed a City but Couldn't Digest It.
summary: CGP Grey explains that the City of London is a tiny, separate entity with its own governance, history and privileges, distinct from the city called London. He covers its financial role and how it is run.
why_hn: HN's go-to short explainer for the City of London versus London, cited in many finance and UK threads.

quote.text: CGP Grey has a delightful video explaining this

title: Preventing the Collapse of Civilization / Jonathan Blow (Thekla, Inc)
summary: A DevGAMM talk by Jonathan Blow arguing that civilizations can lose technological capability and that software quality is already deteriorating. He discusses how knowledge fails to transfer between generations.
why_hn: It is the standard link in HN threads about software decay, lost knowledge and fragile technological civilization.

quote.text: Anyone who finds this concept interesting to think about and hasn't seen this video may enjoy it

title: Conway's Game Of Life in APL
summary: A short Dyalog demonstration building Conway's Game of Life in a single line of APL, step by step. It shows how array operations replace loops.
why_hn: Recommended whenever APL or array languages come up as the quickest way to see why the paradigm is so striking.

quote.text: Try watching this video; it will only take you 8 minutes

title: Finding the Missing Memristor - R. Stanley Williams
summary: R. Stanley Williams of HP Labs gives a keynote on the memristor, covering the physics, crossbar computation, and potential for memory and new computer architectures.
why_hn: Recommended for years as the best technical introduction to memristors from the person who found the physical device.

quote.text: I encourage folks to watch this tech talk by HP Research Labs on the discovery of the memristor and implementation details.

title: Winners Take All | Anand Giridharadas | Talks at Google
summary: Anand Giridharadas presents his book Winners Take All at Google, arguing that the global elite's philanthropy and 'win-win' framing preserve the systems that create inequity. He challenges the audience, including Google employees, to examine their own role in that system.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a pointed critique of philanthropy and win-win thinking, delivered inside Google itself, and cite it across threads on wealth, tax and tech power.

quote.text: I strongly encourage everyone - especialy anyone employed at Google - to watch it.

title: Ed Catmull, Pixar: Keep Your Crises Small
summary: Ed Catmull of Pixar speaks at Stanford's 2007 Entrepreneurship Conference on running a creative company. He argues for surfacing small problems early and building good teams, with stories like the Toy Story 2 crunch.
why_hn: Repeatedly called one of the most useful talks on building organizations and managing creative teams.

quote.text: one of the most useful talks of all time for building organizations is by Ed Catmull (of Pixar)

title: "Performance Matters" by Emery Berger
summary: Emery Berger explains why performance is hard to measure and deliver on modern hardware, showing how code layout and alignment can swamp optimization effects. He presents Stabilizer for statistically sound evaluation and Coz, a causal profiler.
why_hn: It is the standard recommendation for anyone puzzled by unexplained benchmark changes from tiny code edits, and for learning about causal profiling.

quote.text: this is the most amazing optimisation information I have seen

title: Alain de Botton: Status Anxiety
summary: Alain de Botton's 2004 documentary based on his book Status Anxiety, running over two hours. It asks why people in rich societies are still unhappy, and examines how worries about success, snobbery and meritocracy drive that anxiety.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an illuminating, eye-opening long-form take on status, luck and how we judge the successful and unsuccessful.

quote.text: This doc is eye-opening

title: [LIVE] How to Achieve Proper Grounding - Rick Hartley - Expert Live Training (US)
summary: Rick Hartley gives a roughly two-hour live training on proper grounding in PCB design. He explains how energy actually flows in the space between conductors, and how that governs noise, EMI, return paths and signal reflections.
why_hn: Hailed as the best video on electrical engineering and an essential, eye-opening watch for anyone designing high-speed boards.

quote.text: the best video I've ever seen on electrical engineering

title: The Antique Toaster that's Better than Yours
summary: Technology Connections takes apart a 1940s Sunbeam Radiant Control toaster. It senses the toast's own browning and lowers and raises it automatically using purely mechanical parts and no electronics.
why_hn: HN returns to it again and again as a favorite example of elegant, chip-free mechanical engineering that beats modern toasters.

quote.text: In case you haven't seen this video of a toaster from the 60s before, you're in for a treat

title: Lecture 1A | MIT 6.001 Structure and Interpretation, 1986
summary: The first lecture of MIT's 1986 6.001 Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, given by Harold Abelson, introducing Lisp and the idea of computer science as the study of process.
why_hn: Seen as a classic and often the moment programming 'clicks'; commenters praise Abelson's opening that computer science is not about computers.

quote.text: blew my mind and made me switch from being a UX designer dabbling in Rails to a full blown programmer.

title: Christopher Hitchens - Free Speech
summary: Christopher Hitchens delivers a speech defending freedom of speech, including the right of audiences to hear offensive speakers and a take on the fire-in-a-crowded-theatre line. It is framed around the Charlie Hebdo attack.
why_hn: HN invokes it in nearly every content moderation and censorship thread as the most eloquent case for free speech.

quote.text: There is a brilliant speech by the late Christopher Hitchens [0] on free speech that I must have seen a dozen times.

title: Painting a Character with Maths
summary: Inigo Quilez live-codes a cartoon character painting entirely from math, using signed distance fields in a Shadertoy shader. He explains each step of building the image from formulas.
why_hn: HN repeatedly calls it a mind-blowing and accessible introduction to SDFs and procedural art from a master explainer.

quote.text: he's a master of this stuff and a great explainer.

title: The Most IMPORTANT Video You'll Ever See (part 1 of 8)
summary: Part 1 of a lecture by physicist Albert Bartlett on the exponential function and its consequences for population growth, resource use and energy. It argues that steady growth rates quickly lead to enormous quantities.
why_hn: A perennial HN recommendation for building intuition about exponential growth, cited whenever endless growth, energy or population come up.

quote.text: stick with it; it's really captivating and interesting

title: Alan Kay - Normal Considered Harmful
summary: Alan Kay's 2009 UIUC talk arguing that computing is more a pop culture than a science and that ignoring history and fundamentals leads to inferior solutions. He touches on the history of interactive environments and what the web should have been.
why_hn: A staple on must-watch lists, recommended as a starting point for Kay's thinking and for why software is often poor and ahistorical.

quote.text: his talk 'Normal Considered Harmful' in particular is worth a look as it pretty much goes straight to the heart of the issue

title: Antonin Scalia - On American Exceptionalism
summary: Justice Antonin Scalia's opening statement at a 2011 Senate Judiciary hearing on the role of judges. He argues that the Constitution's separation of powers is what protects liberty, and that gridlock is by design.
why_hn: Recommended often as a clear explanation of why the US system is built to be slow and why gridlock protects minorities.

quote.text: one of the best explanations for why founding fathers built the system the way they did is this[1], by late Justice Scalia.

title: The Ultimate Game Boy Talk (33c3)
summary: Michael Steil's 33c3 talk explains essentially everything about the Game Boy: CPU, video hardware, peripherals, and the tricks used by games and demos. It revives the era of counting clock cycles around hardware limits.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard starting point for Game Boy emulator writers and homebrew developers, with several calling it one of their favorite talks.

quote.text: I'd recommend watching The Ultimate Game Boy Talk [1] before trying to dive into any code.

title: Crockford on JavaScript - Volume 1: The Early Years
summary: Douglas Crockford's first Yahoo lecture puts JavaScript in historical context. He traces the language's structure and quirks back through the early decades of computer science and programming language history.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends the Crockford series as a must-watch history of computing and programming languages, and as a way to learn to think in JavaScript.
primary_topic: history of javascript and programming languages

quote.text: I urge you to watch this. It really is worth it!

title: Stroads are Ugly, Expensive, and Dangerous (and they're everywhere) [ST05]
summary: Not Just Bikes introduces the "stroad", a street-road hybrid common in the US and Canada that fails at both jobs. He contrasts it with Dutch design, where each road has a single purpose, and covers cost, danger and ugliness.
why_hn: HN links it constantly as the standard introduction to stroads and Strong Towns-style arguments about car-centric design.

quote.text: This video from the Not Just Bikes channel shows the stark difference between a street and a road

title: Controlling Your Dopamine For Motivation, Focus & Satisfaction
summary: Andrew Huberman's long Huberman Lab episode is a masterclass on dopamine. It covers the neural circuits, peaks and baselines, dopamine depletion, and 14 tools for motivation, focus and avoiding addiction.
why_hn: HN recommends it repeatedly to people struggling with motivation, distraction or phone and internet addiction, as a science-based guide to dopamine.

quote.text: I'm obsessed with this podcast by Andrew Huberman (Stanford Neuroscientist) because he's talking about a scientific basis for stuff that has "felt" true to me for a while.

title: RailsConf 2016 -  Turbolinks 5: I Can’t Believe It’s Not Native! by Sam Stephenson
summary: Sam Stephenson's RailsConf 2016 talk on Turbolinks 5, showing how small teams can ship fast Rails apps in the browser and hybrid iOS and Android apps sharing one set of web views.
why_hn: Repeatedly urged on people choosing a stack, as a case against heavy SPA complexity and for shared web and native code.

quote.text: I highly recommend this talk on managing the complexity of basecamp and sharing a codebase between web and native apps.

title: ADHD: Essential Ideas for Parents - Dr. Russell Barkely
summary: Dr. Russell Barkley gives a nearly three-hour lecture of essential ideas about ADHD for parents, covering what ADHD is, its effects on executive function, motivation and emotion, and how it affects children.
why_hn: HN readers recommend it as the best primer for understanding ADHD at a neurological level, often suggesting that even the first 10 to 20 minutes are enlightening.

quote.text: You don't need to watch the entire 3 hours. The first 10 minutes should be fairly enlightening.

title: Growing a Language, by Guy Steele
summary: Guy Steele's 1998 OOPSLA keynote on designing a programming language that its users can grow. He builds the talk using only one-syllable words and terms he has defined, to demonstrate the idea.
why_hn: HN considers it one of the best technical talks ever and cites it in discussions of language design, small cores and extensibility.

quote.text: This is probably the best talk ever on the general topic

title: USENIX Security '18-Q: Why Do Keynote Speakers Keep Suggesting That Improving Security Is Possible?
summary: James Mickens's humorous USENIX Security keynote argues that improving security and trusting opaque technology like machine learning is far harder than the industry admits.
why_hn: HN considers it a classic, hilarious and sobering talk on ML inscrutability and tech hubris, often rewatched.

quote.text: His keynote at USENIX Security 2018 is by far the best summation of the dangers of ML that I've ever seen.

title: A Philosophy of Software Design | John Ousterhout | Talks at Google
summary: John Ousterhout, Stanford professor and creator of Tcl, presents the ideas of his book A Philosophy of Software Design in a Talks at Google session. He covers managing complexity, deep modules and interfaces, and what he teaches in his Stanford software design course.
why_hn: HN treats it as the standard one-hour teaser for the book and recommends it for its deep-modules thinking before buying or reading the book.

quote.text: This google talk is a condensed version of the (already small - 150 pags IIRC) book. I highly recommend both.

title: Defcon 18   Changing threats to privacy   Moxie Marlinspike   Part
summary: Moxie Marlinspike's DEF CON 18 talk on changing threats to privacy argues that surveillance arrived through convenient services and network effects, so opting out is not a real solution. It also includes his framing of getting social democracy rather than the fascism people feared.
why_hn: Cited repeatedly to rebut 'just don't use Facebook' arguments and to explain why tracking becomes hard to escape at critical mass.

quote.text: I would highly encourage anyone who thinks that the solution is as simple as "don't use XYZ" to see what Moxie Marlinspike had to say

title: "Uncle" Bob Martin - "The Future of Programming"
summary: Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob) traces the history of software from 1948 to today, looking at the problems programmers faced, how they were solved, and what mistakes the profession made. He then projects where the field is going, including professionalism and regulation.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an engaging overview of programming history and an argument for professional standards, citing the agile manifesto section and the claim that software has advanced little since the 1950s.

quote.text: It's a fascinating introduction to the evolution of hardware and programming languages.

title: The Thirty Million Line Problem
summary: Casey Muratori's long talk arguing that modern software has ballooned to tens of millions of lines because of hardware and OS diversity. He proposes a stable ISA for entire system-on-a-chip packages and recalls when games shipped with their own boot disk.
why_hn: HN recommends it, long as it is, as an eye-opening rant on software complexity and why systems became so complicated.

quote.text: The video is long, but it's worth watching all of it.

title: CppCon 2017: Matt Kulukundis “Designing a Fast, Efficient, Cache-friendly Hash Table, Step by Step”
summary: Matt Kulukundis explains how Google designed SwissTable, a fast, cache-friendly hash table, step by step from std::unordered_map. The talk covers open addressing, SIMD probing and the tradeoffs of changing a fundamental data structure.
why_hn: HN repeatedly cites it as the definitive explanation of SwissTable, the design behind Abseil, Rust's hash map and Go's maps.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: Excellent talk which explains the concepts really clearly and concisely.

title: The Cardboard Box Reform - Nixon's Ghost Bill & A Crucial Flaw in Democracy
summary: James D'Angelo argues that the 1970 Legislative Reorganization Act made congressional votes public, opening the door to lobbyists and special interests. He proposes restoring secret voting as a cheap fix for corruption and many social ills.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a long, evidence-backed theory for what changed in the 1970s and why Congress is broken, even when they are unsure they agree.

quote.text: It is long, but well-reasoned and supported by a lot of evidence. Definitely worth a watch...

title: Effective Programs - 10 Years of Clojure - Rich Hickey
summary: Rich Hickey's talk at Clojure's tenth anniversary on the kind of programs Clojure is designed for. He argues for situated programs that deal with changing requirements, and for dynamic typing and data over static types.
why_hn: HN's go-to link in typing debates and for talk lists, and several call it their favorite programming talk even for non-Clojure users.

quote.text: Whole video is gold, is my fav programming talk of all time.

title: Brian Goetz - Stewardship: the Sobering Parts
summary: Java Language Architect Brian Goetz talks at a Clojure conference about the challenges of evolving a mature language like Java while preserving compatibility with existing code and developer expectations. It also gives a look at where the platform is headed.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the definitive explanation of why Java evolves cautiously and why compatibility matters in language design.

quote.text: Brian Goetz's talk nails it on the head why the languages in my day-to-day are sub-optimal

title: Music and Life - Alan Watts
summary: A two-minute animation of an Alan Watts talk arguing that life is like music: it is meant to be danced to in the moment, not rushed toward a final goal. It is a short, accessible take on living in the present.
why_hn: HN commenters post it in threads about purpose, ambition, burnout and career anxiety as a reframing that life is a dance, not a march toward eventual happiness.

quote.text: You haven't been failing, you've been dancing.

title: VCF East: Ken Thompson interviewed by Brian Kernighan
summary: Brian Kernighan interviews Unix co-creator Ken Thompson at VCF East 2019. Thompson recounts how he was hired at Bell Labs, writing the Unix kernel in about three weeks, the origins of B and TMG, pipes, and other anecdotes.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for Thompson's funny, first-hand Unix history stories, some of which even Kernighan had not heard.

quote.text: Also I found these fascinating

title: AWS re:Invent 2018: Amazon DynamoDB Deep Dive: Advanced Design Patterns for DynamoDB (DAT401)
summary: Rick Houlihan's AWS re:Invent 2018 deep dive on advanced DynamoDB design patterns. It covers index overloading, GSI sharding, composite keys, graph processing and transactions.
why_hn: The go-to recommendation for learning DynamoDB data modeling, with many saying it made access-pattern-driven design click.

quote.text: I highly recommend every engineer to watch it: it's a great overview of SQL vs NoSQL

title: Harder Drive: Hard drives we didn't want or need
summary: Tom7 (suckerpinch) builds and evaluates a series of absurd hard drives, including storage made from ping packets across the internet. The video accompanies his paper and mixes deep technical hacking with comedic storytelling.
why_hn: HN treats it as a favorite example of silly but educational computer science, recommended often when threads touch odd storage hacks.

quote.text: recommend this video to anyone here.

title: Breakthrough in  Nuclear Fusion? - Prof. Dennis Whyte
summary: MIT's Prof. Dennis Whyte explains the ARC/SPARC compact tokamak approach, in which new high-temperature superconducting magnets allow smaller and cheaper fusion reactors. He covers fusion physics, performance trends and the engineering path to net energy.
why_hn: HN points to it as the grounded, approachable explanation of why REBCO magnets changed the outlook for fusion.

quote.text: I highly recommend watching Dr. Whyte's talks on YouTube, he discusses the challenges, design, and performance in an approachable way.

title: The Solar Gravitational Lens will Map Exoplanets. Seriously.
summary: Explains the proposed NASA JPL plan to use the Sun as a gravitational lens, sending solar sail craft to its focal region to image an exoplanet's surface. It covers the distances involved, how imaging with the Sun would work and the mission design.

summary: Lawrence Krauss's 2009 talk on the current picture of the universe, how it will end and how it could have come from nothing. It covers the expanding universe, cosmic background radiation and the cosmological constant.
